The best wildlife around Koh Samui is in the sea and on the outer islands rather than on Samui itself. Pink (Indo-Pacific humpback) dolphins feed off the mainland coast south-west of the island and are the focus of our Pink Dolphins and Pig Island tour (2,250 THB); reef fish, and occasionally turtles, live around Ang Thong, Koh Tan and Koh Nang Yuan; and whale sharks are sometimes seen at Sail Rock. Ang Thong Marine Park, closed 1 November–15 December 2026, is home to dusky leaf monkeys, long-tailed macaques, otters, sea eagles and hornbills. On Samui you will mostly see geckos, monitor lizards, squirrels and birds. Avoid any venue that offers elephant riding or bathing, animal shows or photo props.

Pink dolphins off the south-west coast

The "pink dolphins" of the Gulf of Thailand are Indo-Pacific humpback dolphins (Sousa chinensis). They are grey when young and often turn pink as they age, and they live in shallow coastal water near river mouths. The group most often seen on day trips from Samui feeds off the Khanom coast on the mainland, about 45 minutes by speedboat from Thong Krut. The species is listed as Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List, threatened mainly by fishing nets, coastal development and boat traffic.

Seeing them on our tour

The Pink Dolphins and Pig Island tour (2,250 THB, about 6 hours) crosses to the dolphins' usual feeding grounds, where a captain who knows the area looks for them, then snorkels the reef at Koh Tan and visits the pigs on Koh Madsum. The dolphins are wild, so sightings are not guaranteed; the order of stops depends on the tide, the wind and where the dolphins are that morning. Calm seas give the best chance of spotting fins, so book early in your stay to leave room for a second try on another day.

Watching dolphins responsibly

  • The boat slows well before the dolphins and keeps a respectful distance.
  • It never chases, cuts across or circles a group, and goes to neutral or switches off when dolphins come close.
  • No swimming with the dolphins and no feeding.
  • Bring polarised sunglasses to see under the glare, and a zoom lens: dolphins surface briefly and at a distance.

Reef life at Ang Thong, Koh Tan and Sail Rock

Koh Tan and Pig Island

Koh Tan has the best easy reef close to Samui: a shallow reef along Ao Ok beach with patchy hard coral and reef fish, at depths where most people can see the bottom without diving. Dynamite fishing damaged reefs in this area until about the 1980s; parts have recovered, but expect patchy coral rather than a wall of colour, and turtles are rare. It is on every Pig Island trip and runs all year.

Ang Thong Marine Park

Ang Thong's 42 islands have shallow fringing reefs on their sheltered sides, with hard corals and reef fish; green and hawksbill turtles and yellow-spotted trevally are on the park's records. Visibility drops after rain, when run-off from the islands clouds the water. The park is closed every year from 1 November to 15 December and reopens on 16 December; the cash park fee is 300 THB per foreign adult and 150 THB per child. Snorkelling is part of the speedboat tour (1,800 THB) and the big boat tour (1,500 THB).

Sail Rock and Koh Tao

Sail Rock, a granite pinnacle between Koh Phangan and Koh Tao, is the Gulf's best dive site from Samui: barracuda, batfish, trevally and giant groupers circle the rock, and whale sharks visit occasionally. Treat a whale shark as a bonus, not a promise. Snorkellers can join some Sail Rock days, though it is a deep, open-water site best suited to divers; the shallow Japanese Gardens at Koh Nang Yuan suit snorkellers better. See diving from Koh Samui and snorkelling, or book the Sail Rock and Koh Tao catamaran day (snorkelling 2,900 THB).

Reef rules

  • Don't stand on, touch or kick coral: it injures you and kills the reef. Practise floating in a life jacket if you are unsure.
  • Use reef-safe mineral sunscreen; oxybenzone and similar filters are banned in national parks, including Ang Thong. A rash vest is better still.
  • Don't feed fish, chase turtles or pick up shells, starfish or sea cucumbers.
  • Wear water shoes on rocky entries: sea urchins live in crevices and coral cuts infect easily.

Ang Thong's wildlife on land

Ang Thong is the best place near Samui for land wildlife, because the islands are protected forest with no roads. The park has recorded 16 mammal species, about 50 bird species and 14 reptiles. On a day trip you are most likely to see:

  • Dusky leaf monkeys (langurs): grey with white "spectacles" around the eyes, feeding quietly in the forest canopy. Shy and gentle.
  • Long-tailed macaques: bolder, and they will grab food and bags. Don't feed them or carry food openly.
  • Birds: white-bellied sea eagles and brahminy kites over the cliffs, collared kingfishers along the shore, Pacific reef herons on the rocks and, with luck, oriental pied hornbills.
  • Others on the park's list: smooth-coated otters, wild boar, leopard cats and fishing cats, though these are rarely seen by day visitors.

Some birds on the list, such as the black baza and the Eurasian woodcock, are migrants that winter in southern Thailand [check]. Feeding wild animals in a national park is prohibited. The overnight camping trip gives you dawn and dusk on Koh Wua Talab, when wildlife is most active.

Jungle animals on Koh Samui

Samui's interior is a patchwork of coconut plantations, fruit orchards and forest on the higher hills, so wildlife is mostly small and used to people.

  • Geckos: small house geckos on every wall at night, and the larger tokay gecko, whose loud "to-kay" call you will hear after dark. Both eat insects and are harmless; leave them alone.
  • Monitor lizards: water monitors live around canals, ponds and mangroves, and can reach well over a metre. They are shy and will move away if you give them space; never corner or feed one.
  • Squirrels: several species run along power lines and coconut palms.
  • Birds: mynas, bulbuls and sunbirds in gardens; kingfishers and herons along streams and the coast.
  • Insects and spiders: butterflies are abundant in the green season; centipedes and scorpions occasionally turn up in damp places, so shake out shoes and towels.
  • Monkeys: wild troops are rarely seen in the tourist areas of Samui itself. Macaques you see on Samui are usually working or captive animals (see below).

The best way to see Samui's forest is on foot: the trails to Hin Lad waterfall and Na Muang 2 pass through jungle, and our hiking guide lists routes and safety tips.

Birdwatching

Samui isn't a major birding destination, but a pair of binoculars pays off. Early morning is best, before 08:30. On the coast, look for white-bellied sea eagles and brahminy kites soaring over headlands, and herons and egrets on the tidal flats at low tide on the north and west coasts. In gardens and plantations you'll hear bulbuls and mynas and see sunbirds feeding on flowers. For forest species such as hornbills and the black baza, Ang Thong's islands give the best odds, especially on an overnight trip when you're on the island at dawn.

Wildlife photography tips

  • Use a zoom of at least 200 mm for dolphins and birds; dolphins surface briefly, so shoot in bursts.
  • A polarising filter or polarised sunglasses cut surface glare at sea.
  • For reef photos, a phone in a waterproof case works well in the shallows at Koh Tan; shoot near the surface with the sun behind you.
  • Never bait, touch or move animals for a picture, and don't use flash on monkeys, owls or nocturnal animals.

Snakes and safety

Snakes live on Samui, as everywhere in tropical Thailand, but visitors rarely see them, and bites are uncommon. Most snakes are shy and move away when they feel footsteps. Venomous species found in southern Thailand include cobras, kraits and pit vipers, while many snakes seen around gardens, such as rat snakes and the golden tree snake, are harmless or only mildly venomous [check].

  • Walk on paths, wear closed shoes on jungle trails and use a torch at night.
  • Don't put your hands into holes, under rocks or into piles of leaves and coconut husks.
  • If you see a snake, back away slowly and let it go. Hotels and villa managers can call a local snake catcher.

If someone is bitten

  1. Keep the person calm and still, and call the ambulance on 1669.
  2. Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint or sling, and remove rings and watches.
  3. Don't cut, suck, apply a tight tourniquet, ice or herbal remedies.
  4. Take a photo of the snake only if you can do it safely; doctors treat by symptoms.
  5. Go straight to a hospital with a 24-hour emergency department. See hospitals on Koh Samui.

Jellyfish and other sea stingers

Box jellyfish are rare but dangerous in the Gulf of Thailand. Of the first 10 box jellyfish deaths recorded in Thailand since 2002, 9 were in waters off Samui and Koh Phangan, and on 1 August 2026 a 13-year-old boy died after a sting at Sichon on the mainland coast, after which the Department of Marine and Coastal Resources stepped up monitoring and warnings. Risk is higher in calm, warm water after rain and around dusk. Swim in netted areas where they exist, and look for vinegar stations on hotel beaches.

First aid: get the person out of the water, pour household vinegar over the sting for at least 30 seconds, don't rub and don't rinse with fresh water, then call 1669. Watch for breathing problems and start CPR if needed. Sea urchin spines and coral cuts are much more common: wear water shoes, and clean any cut thoroughly. Full advice is in beach safety on Koh Samui.

Elephants: the ethical rules

Elephants are not native wildlife on Samui today: the animals on the island are domestic, and many were retired from logging, trekking or street work elsewhere in Thailand. How they are treated depends entirely on the venue. Our rules, which are also the rules we sell by:

  • No riding, with or without a seat.
  • No bathing or swimming with tourists.
  • No shows, painting, tricks or performances.
  • No hooks or chains on show during the visit, and space for elephants to roam and forage.
  • Visitors observe, prepare food and feed from a safe position, guided by staff.

How to judge a venue is covered in our ethical elephant sanctuary guide. Visits that meet this standard include the hands-off skywalk sanctuary visit (3,000 THB, child 1,700 THB), where you watch the herd from a raised walkway, and the Bophut hills sanctuary (from 2,000 THB, child 1,000 THB) for feeding and walking with the elephants. Even at good sanctuaries, feeding means the elephants are habituated to people; no Samui venue is a wild release project, and we say so honestly.

Animal attractions to avoid

  • Elephant riding or bathing, and the chained elephants offered for feeding or photos at roadside viewpoints.
  • Tiger and big-cat attractions: Samui Aquarium and Tiger Zoo had no confirmed opening in 2026, and captive tigers raised for visitor contact have long drawn welfare concerns.
  • Snake, crocodile and monkey shows, including snake shows and "snake farms" of the old kind; Samui Snake Farm was unconfirmed in 2026.
  • Macaques in chains or costumes, including "coconut monkey" shows for tourists. Pig-tailed macaques have long been trained to pick coconuts in southern Thailand, and animal-welfare groups have criticised how they are kept and trained.
  • Photo props: slow lorises, baby gibbons, iguanas or birds offered for photos on beaches and in bars. These are often illegally taken from the wild, and paying keeps the trade going.
  • Namuang Safari Park: its old listings advertised elephant rides and animal shows; the site now trades as an elephant venue we have not been able to verify.

The Pig Island pigs

The pigs on Koh Madsum are domestic animals that live on the beach and wade into the shallows. They are well known and photographed, so behave as you would with any animal: let them come to you, don't chase, lift or ride them, and leave the piglets alone. Feed only what island staff provide, if anything, and never crisps, bread or sweets. Give them space in the midday heat, when they rest in the shade. The island charges a fee of about 50 THB per person, paid in cash.

Stray dogs and cats, and how to help

Samui has many free-roaming dogs and cats. Most beach dogs are calm and are fed by local shops and temples, but packs can be territorial at night, particularly on quiet roads and beaches.

  • Don't approach, pet or feed unknown dogs; walk calmly and don't run.
  • Carry a stick or umbrella on quiet night walks, and cross the road away from a pack.
  • Rabies is present in Thailand. After any bite or scratch from a dog, cat or monkey, wash the wound with soap and running water for 15 minutes and go to a hospital the same day for rabies treatment, even if you were vaccinated before.

To help, donate to or volunteer with a registered local charity. The Samui Dog and Cat Rescue Centre is a non-profit foundation that looks after the island's stray dogs and cats. Don't take in or relocate street animals yourself without advice.

Protected species and the law

Thailand's Wild Animal Conservation and Protection Act B.E. 2562 (2019) protects most native wildlife, and the National Parks Act covers everything inside parks such as Ang Thong. In practice, for visitors:

  • Don't buy, collect or export coral, shells, turtle shell, ivory, wild-animal products or live animals; customs at home may seize them too.
  • Don't feed, touch or disturb wildlife in national parks, and don't take anything from them, including sand, coral or plants.
  • Don't pay for photos with wild animals or buy "wild" pets.
  • Report wildlife for sale or injured protected animals to the Department of National Parks, Wildlife and Plant Conservation (dnp.go.th) or the Tourist Police on 1155.
